source.title: Neuron with Steady Response Leads to Better Generalization
source.authors: Qiang Fu; Lun Du; Hai-Tao Mao; Xu Chen; W. Fang; Shi Han; Dong-Mei Zhang

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied, including appendices; no truncation apparent.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether a measured property of trained networks tracks generalization and whether explicitly regularizing that property improves test error; this is a conceptual test of the catalog claim, not its random-label or other listed interventions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results on class-dependent neuron response variance and test error after adding NSR. Results in cited work are not counted. The training-curve figures are described in text, but precise values visible only in the figures are not reconstructed.
record.test_reason: Table 5 directly compares dropout with no dropout on an MNIST fully connected classifier, measuring held-out error as in V6. The main NSR experiments measure response variance and regularization benefits, not V7's magnitude-aware weight-perturbation sharpness.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is substantially accurate: the authors associate lower intra-class neuron response variance with classification correctness and report that NSR improves held-out performance across MLP, CNN, and GNN experiments. Their theoretical argument concerns a representation-based complexity measure, not magnitude-aware sharpness.
record.recipe_differences: Adds explicit neuron intra-class response variance regularization to cross-entropy training; uses standard optimizers and benchmark evaluation rather than random-label, width, architecture-comparison, optimizer, batch-size, dropout, magnitude-aware sharpness, or memorized-example interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: The layer selected for NSR changes the measured error; the authors report that the layer with the largest aggregated variance gives the strongest individual-layer gain in the tested MLP-4 and GraphSAGE-2 comparisons. They also report outliers in GraphSAGE response-variance dynamics.

fits_no_version.finding: NSR controls intra-class neuron response variance during training and accompanies improved test performance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Penalizing class-dependent neuron response variance can improve classification performance; response variance is distinct from weight-perturbation sharpness.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding NSR lowers reported error across the recorded MLP, CNN, and GNN comparisons.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: NSR can improve held-out classification performance in the tested architectures and datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding NSR to BN or dropout further lowers MLP-4 error on MNIST.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: NSR can provide additional benefits alongside BN or dropout.

fits_no_version.finding: NSR's benefit varies with the layer selected; the highest-variance layer gives the best reported individual-layer result.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Layer selection affects NSR performance, and selecting the highest-response-variance layer works well in these two examples.

record.problems: The paper tests NSR and class-dependent response variance, not the magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness measure in V7; it does not directly measure training-test gaps. Some variance results are figure-only without exact values. Several reported comparisons are limited to individual datasets and architectures; the paper states GraphSAGE variance curves have a few outliers.
record.rows_left_out: No reported results on the eight remaining catalog versions were found. The MLP and CNN training-dynamics figures for other conditions and the memory-queue-length accuracy plot (Figures 2, 4, 5, and 6) are figure-only; only the directly described dynamics for the three architecture examples are retained, while Figure 6 tests queue length rather than a catalog version.

untested.parts: Random-label memorization and its coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Width beyond the zero-training-error threshold; the paper varies depth instead.
Controlled convolutional versus fully connected comparisons and the role of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer comparisons under matched tuning.
Large-batch penalties under fixed epoch budgets and compensating recipes. Figure 6 studies queue length with several modest batch sizes.
Dropout in convolutional classifiers, very small training sets, excessive dropout, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay with augmentation.
All: magnitude-scaled weight perturbations, generalization-gap rankings, and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Identifying and removing memorized training examples versus random removal.

record.verdict_notes: The record overlooks the direct dropout-only result in Table 5. Its V7 links should all be removed. R11 needs to separate the dropout-only comparison from the additional NSR intervention; the V6 verdict rests on the former.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out performance on natural labels.
Width sweep beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons and local connectivity.
Large versus small batch generalization gap.
Dropout’s effect as an intervention, including small-data and underfitting regimes.
Magnitude-scaled perturbation sharpness, comparison with norm- and margin-based measures, CIFAR-10/SVHN scope, and the cited sharpness counterexamples.
Removing memorized examples and measuring resulting test accuracy.

rows.note: Authors state that NSR controls and reduces response variance after a few epochs and that its model has higher testing accuracy than vanilla, despite higher cross-entropy loss.
